system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 19 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 60-85 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2150-11-18 13:52:00 to 2150-12-07 11:27:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: The patient was admitted for an allogeneic stem cell transplant from her matched sister following complete remission from CML in myeloblastic crisis. She underwent myeloablative conditioning with fludarabine and busulfan, followed by stem cell infusion on day 6. The hospital course was complicated by neutropenic fever, nausea, vomiting, mucositis, headaches, and a presyncopal episode due to dehydration. She required IV hydration and antiemetic adjustments. Multiple central lines were placed and repositioned as needed. No infections were identified on repeated cultures. Engraftment occurred by day +15, with improving counts and resolution of symptoms. Discharge was delayed due to persistent nausea but was achieved on day +23 with plans for home IV support and close outpatient follow-up.
problems: Chronic myeloid leukemia, without mention of having achieved remission
Nausea with vomiting
Mucositis (ulcerative) due to antineoplastic therapy
Abdominal pain, unspecified site
Fever presenting with conditions classified elsewhere
Dermatitis due to drugs and medicines taken internally
Esophageal reflux
Internal hemorrhoids without mention of complication
Antineoplastic and immunosuppressive drugs causing adverse effects in therapeutic use

radiology_notes.text:
TWO-VIEW CHEST RADIOGRAPH ___

COMPARISON:  ___

INDICATION:  PICC.

FINDINGS:  Left PICC terminates just below the expected location of the
junction of the superior vena cava and right atrium.  Cardiac silhouette is
upper limits of normal in size but stable from the prior study.  Small
calcified granuloma is present in the right mid lung.  Lungs are otherwise
clear and there are no pleural effusions or acute skeletal findings.

Comparison is also made to CT of the abdomen dated ___, confirming
the tip of the PICC catheter within the right atrium.

IMPRESSION:  PICC terminates below the junction of the superior vena cava and
right atrium, with tip confirmed in the body of the right atrium by review of
abdominal CT ___.

INDICATION:  ___ woman with diarrhea and diffuse abdominal pain, with
bone marrow transplant one month ago and history of prior typhlitis.

COMPARISON:  ___.

TECHNIQUE:  MDCT-acquired axial images were obtained through the abdomen and
pelvis following the administration of intravenous contrast material.
Multiplanar reformatted images were generated.

CT ABDOMEN WITH IV CONTRAST:  Lung bases demonstrate mild dependent
atelectasis, without consolidation or pleural effusion.  The heart is normal
in size without pericardial effusion.  Catheter terminates in the distal SVC.
Calcified left hilar nodes are consistent with prior granulomatous disease.  A
coarse calcification in the right medial breast is unchanged.

In the abdomen, the patient is post-cholecystectomy with clips in the
gallbladder fossa.  The liver, pancreas (demonstrating mild fatty
replacement), spleen (with focal calcification consistent with granulomatous
disease unchanged), adrenal glands, stomach and duodenum are unremarkable. The
kidneys enhance and excrete contrast symmetrically without hydronephrosis or
renal masses.  The abdominal aorta and its major branches are within normal
limits.  There is no mesenteric or retroperitoneal lymphadenopathy by size
criteria.  There is no free air or free fluid in the abdomen.

CT PELVIS WITH IV CONTRAST:  Since the prior study ___, findings
consistent with diffuse colitis have developed, including prominent wall
thickening and edema involving the terminal ileum, cecum, ascending,
transverse and sigmoid colon, and to a lesser degree, the rectum.  There is
mild mesenteric stranding adjacent to the colon.  The appendix is normal.
There is a small amount of free fluid dependently within the pelvis.  There is
no evidence of perforation.  Scattered diverticula are noted of the sigmoid
colon, without focal inflammatory changes to suggest diverticulitis.

The urinary bladder, distal ureters, uterus and adnexa are unremarkable. There
is no pelvic or inguinal lymphadenopathy by size criteria.

OSSEOUS STRUCTURES:  There is no worrisome bony lesion.  No fractures are
present.  Soft tissues are unremarkable.

IMPRESSION:
Diffuse colitis and terminal ileitis, consistent with infection.  C. diff is a
possible etiologic agent.  Typhlitis not likely due to distribution and
particularly if the patient is not neutropenic, as current lab results
indicate.

TWO-VIEW CHEST, ___

COMPARISON:  ___.

INDICATION:  White blood cell elevation.

FINDINGS:  Cardiac silhouette is mildly enlarged.  Lungs are clear except for
a linear opacity in the right upper lobe and a small calcified granuloma.  No
pleural effusion or acute skeletal abnormality.

PICC terminates in region of junction of superior vena cava and right atrium.

IMPRESSION:  Small linear opacity in right upper lobe suggestive of linear
atelectasis.  No consolidation to suggest infectious pneumonia.  Incidental
calcified granuloma, unchanged.

HISTORY:  ___ woman with pancolitis, status post colonoscopy,
concerning for perforation.

Supine and upright abdominal radiographs were obtained.

COMPARISON:  CT abdomen, ___.

FINDINGS:  There is no free air.  There is a nonspecific non-obstructive bowel
gas pattern.  There are surgical clips distributed in the patient's right
upper quadrant related to prior cholecystectomy.  There are mild degenerative
changes of the lower lumbar spine.  The visualized lung bases appear clear.

IMPRESSION:

No free air.  No bowel obstruction.

CT ABDOMEN AND PELVIS WITH INTRAVENOUS CONTRAST

INDICATION:  ___ woman with pancolitis, status post colonoscopy, with
continued abdominal pain, concern for perforation versus worsening colitis.

COMPARISON:  ___.

TECHNIQUE:  MDCT axial images of the abdomen and pelvis were obtained
following administration of intravenous contrast as well as Gastrografin
orally.  Coronal and sagittal reformatted images were obtained.

CT ABDOMEN WITH INTRAVENOUS CONTRAST:  There is a new small left pleural
effusion.  Adjacent trace atelectasis is seen.

The liver enhances heterogeneously.  The main portal vein is patent, as well
as IVC and hepatic veins.

There is significant increase in abdominal ascites.  Spleen, pancreas, adrenal
glands are unremarkable.  The patient is post-cholecystectomy.  The kidneys
enhance equally and excrete contrast normally.  The abdominal aorta is normal
in caliber.

Again noted is wall thickening and edema involving the terminal ileum, cecum,
ascending, transverse and sigmoid colon.  In presence of ascites, mesenteric
stranding adjacent to the colon is difficult to appreciate.  There is no free
intraperitoneal air or extraluminal contrast.  Again noted are scattered
diverticuli of the sigmoid colon.The appearances in the bowel appear to have
improved overall

CT PELVIS WITH INTRAVENOUS CONTRAST:  The uterus, urinary bladder, distal
ureters are unremarkable.  There is a 7-mm focus of high attenuation, appears
to be in the distal anal canal, best seen on series 3A, image 93.This may
represent enhancement or a localized anal process-clinical correlation is
recommended

BONE WINDOWS:  Demonstrate no concerning lytic or sclerotic lesions .

IMPRESSION:
1.  No free intraperitoneal air and no extraluminal contrast; however,
contrast did not progress all the way throughout the large bowel.
2.  Interval significant increase in ascites, new left small pleural effusion.
3.  Abnormal heterogeneous enhancement of the liver, correlate with liver
function tests.
4.  Slight improvement in pancolitis and distal ileitis.

COMPARISONS:  Comparison to recent CT examination from ___.

DOPPLER EXAMINATION:  The right, left, and middle hepatic veins are patent

the left portal vein are patent with appropriate directions of flow.  The

There is a stable appearance of probable hepatic enlargement with inferior tip

IMPRESSION:
1.  Unremarkable Doppler ultrasound examination with patent hepatic

2.  Small amount of ascites is unchanged.  Appearance of probable mild liver

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I understand you were just readmitted after being home for only a few hours. Can you tell me what happened?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I got home around 7 last night. By midnight, I started feeling really sick—nausea, vomiting, and terrible cramping in my belly. The diarrhea was watery, no blood, but it was constant.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And how does the pain compare to what you had before?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It’s worse—same kind of crampy pain, but much stronger. I didn’t take my temperature, but I don’t feel feverish.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. The nurse mentioned you didn’t take any of your medications at home, including tacrolimus. Is that right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, my husband and I were confused about the list. We didn’t want to take the wrong thing, so we waited. I didn’t even take my evening dose.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s understandable, but tacrolimus is critical to prevent graft rejection. We’ll make sure you have a clear plan before going home again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I didn’t realize it was that important. I’m sorry.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No need to apologize. We’ll get you back on track. For now, we’ve made you NPO—nothing by mouth—so your gut can rest.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So no food or water?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not for now. We’ll give you fluids and nutrition through your IV. We also ordered a CT scan of your abdomen to see what’s going on.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your CT scan is back. It shows pancolitis—widespread inflammation of the colon. We need to figure out if it’s infection, GVHD, or something else.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that related to the transplant?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. GVHD can affect the gut. But we also need to rule out infections like C. diff, which is common after antibiotics.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had C. diff before. Is that what this is?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your stool test was negative for C. diff toxin, so probably not. We’ll do a colonoscopy tomorrow to get tissue samples.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We reviewed your labs. Your tacrolimus level this morning was 10.6—on the higher side. That could be contributing to nausea and gut issues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So the medicine meant to help is making me sick?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It can, especially at high levels. We’re going to adjust the dose down and monitor you closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The colonoscopy is done. Good news—no signs of infection or GVHD in the biopsies. The inflammation is there, but not from those causes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So what’s causing it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re not sure yet. It could be drug-related, or part of your immune recovery. We’ll keep watching and adjusting.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re starting parenteral nutrition today. Since you’re not eating, we want to make sure you get proper nutrients through the IV.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I be on this long?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Only until your gut heals enough to handle food. We’ll try small sips soon if things improve.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did another CT today because we noticed your belly is more swollen. There’s new ascites—fluid buildup in the abdomen.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that dangerous?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It can be, so we’re checking for causes—liver issues, heart problems, or infection. The good news is the colitis looks a bit better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So the gut is healing but fluid is building up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. We’ve ordered an echo to check your heart and more blood tests. We’ll keep a close eye.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your echo was normal—no heart failure. Liver ultrasound shows good blood flow, no blockages. The ascites might be related to your medications or immune response.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So what now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re lowering your tacrolimus dose further. It might be contributing to both the gut issues and fluid retention.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your abdominal pain is improving, and the ascites is decreasing. That’s a good sign the dose change is helping.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I try eating something?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ll start with clear liquids—water, broth. If you tolerate that, we’ll advance slowly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great job—you’ve kept down liquids and even a soft diet. Your last tacrolimus level was 2.9, which is much better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I’m healing?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. The pain is gone, your gut is recovering, and the fluid is resolving. We’ll keep monitoring, but you’re on the right track.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your platelets are still low—58,000. We don’t have a clear cause, but we suspect tacrolimus might be playing a role.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that dangerous?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not immediately, but we’ll watch it. We’re not giving any medications that could worsen it, and it may improve as your marrow recovers.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve been stable for two days—eating well, no pain, ambulating. We’re planning for discharge in a couple of days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m nervous about going home again. Last time didn’t go well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Completely understandable. This time, we’ll go over your meds together, and a nurse will review everything with you and your husband.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re updating your medications. You’ll be on mycophenolate and prednisone now, in addition to a lower dose of tacrolimus.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Why the change?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: To better control any immune activity that might be causing gut inflammation, while reducing side effects from high tacrolimus.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: All your recent labs are stable. No signs of infection, CMV is negative, liver tests are improving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the ascites?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Minimal now. Ultrasound showed it hasn’t changed, which means it’s resolving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing so well. We’re scheduling discharge for tomorrow morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about follow-up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll see your transplant team in three days. We’ll check your labs, adjust meds if needed, and monitor your recovery.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Final check—your pain is gone, you’re eating normally, and your vitals are stable. We’ll write your discharge orders today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel so much better than when I came in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I’m glad to hear that. Remember, take all your meds exactly as written. Call us if you develop fever, pain, or can’t keep things down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The nurse will go over your medication list one more time before you leave. Any last questions?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, I think I understand everything now. Thank you for your patience.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re very welcome. You’ve worked hard through this. Take care, and we’ll see you soon in clinic.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You’re cleared to go home. Your condition is stable, and we’re confident you’ll continue to improve.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Dr. Lee. I’m ready to go home—and this time, I’ll take my meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s the plan. Call us with any concerns. Take care, and congratulations on your progress.

summary.summary_paragraph: The patient was readmitted the day after discharge following an allogeneic stem cell transplant for CML in myeloblastic crisis, presenting with severe nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, and worsening abdominal pain. She had not taken her immunosuppressive medications, including tacrolimus, due to confusion at home. Imaging revealed pancolitis and later new ascites. Colonoscopy showed no infection or graft-versus-host disease. Tacrolimus levels were initially high, and dose reduction led to improvement in symptoms and resolution of ascites. She gradually resumed oral intake, remained stable, and was discharged with a revised immunosuppressive regimen including mycophenolate and prednisone. Thrombocytopenia persisted but was stable, likely related to medication effects.
